li.a: NPR: Reuters Publishes Story Of Myanmar Massacre After 2 Journalists Arrested
Al Jazeera: Reuters: Journalists held for probing Rohingya massacre
Al Jazeera: Myanmar soldiers jailed for Rohingya massacre freed after months
Radio Free Asia: Myanmar Opens Rare Court-Martial Case in Army Killings of Rohingya
Radio Free Asia: Myanmar Army Says it Has Convicted Three Troops For 2017 Massacre of Rohingya
Human Rights Watch: Myanmar: Court Martial Latest Accountability Sham
Rappler: Myanmar finds soldiers guilty in Rohingya atrocities court martial

content.p: On 2 September 2017, in a village on the coast of northern Rakhine State, ten Rohingya men and boys were killed and put into a single shallow grave. They had been fishermen, shopkeepers, farmers, two teenage students and an Islamic teacher. Reuters, which reconstructed their last hours five months later, said the killers were Buddhist villagers and Myanmar security forces working side by side. The report rested on photographs of the men kneeling with their hands tied, and of their bodies in the pit.

The village was Inn Din, in Maungdaw township. The killings took place during the military campaign that drove Rohingya out of Rakhine in 2017. They also became a rare case in which the army admitted wrongdoing and punished soldiers, although the punishment lasted less than a year. Meanwhile the two reporters who found the grave served longer in prison than the men convicted of the killings.

Al Jazeera described the 2017 operation as a campaign that spread over hundreds of villages in northern Rakhine, begun after attacks by Rohingya fighters. It drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to Bangladesh. United Nations investigators said it was carried out with "genocidal intent" and involved mass killings, gang rapes and widespread arson. Myanmar denies widespread wrongdoing.

In Inn Din, Reuters reported, troops of the 33rd Light Infantry Division, a mobile force Al Jazeera said had a reputation for brutality, joined paramilitary police and Buddhist vigilantes. Buddhist and Muslim villagers and members of the security forces told Reuters that together they drove out the whole Muslim population, burning and looting homes and property. Paramilitary police gave Reuters what it called insider descriptions of the operation and confirmed that the military had played the lead role.

Reuters said its reconstruction was the first to draw on Buddhist villagers who confessed to burning Rohingya homes, burying bodies and killing Muslims. It also said it was the first time soldiers and paramilitary police had been implicated by testimony from security personnel themselves. Until then, it wrote, accounts of the violence had come only from its victims.

Hundreds of Rohingya men, women and children had fled the burning village and sought safety on a beach, witnesses told Reuters. From that crowd, the report said, ten men were selected. According to Al Jazeera's 2019 summary of the reporting, soldiers and some villagers detained the group on 1 September. The military called the men "terrorists". Their families said they were farmers, high school students and an Islamic teacher.

Abdu Shakur, the father of one of the victims, recalled what the soldiers said as they led the men away. "Don't worry. We will send your sons back soon. We are taking them for a meeting," he told Reuters, in the words reported by Al Jazeera. The victims ranged in age from 17 to 45 and all came from the same Rohingya community in Inn Din.

The next morning, witnesses said, Buddhist villagers hacked some of the men with swords, and Myanmar troops shot the rest. The bodies were buried in a shallow grave. NPR's summary of the Reuters report said the men were killed execution-style. Reuters found witnesses who denied that there had been any major attack by Rohingya militants before the killings, according to Al Jazeera. The military's version was different: it said the men were killed after a massive attack on troops. NPR noted that this did not match any account Reuters heard from paramilitary forces or local villagers.

The images came from a Buddhist village elder, NPR reported. Reuters said he wanted transparency in order to prevent such killings in the future. The journalists identified all ten men in the photographs and spoke to their families and neighbours, now living in refugee camps in Bangladesh, who recognised the victims from the pictures Reuters showed them. Wa Lone also took pictures of the grave site himself.

The finished report was a collaboration of four Reuters journalists: Wa Lone, Kyaw Soe Oo, Simon Lewis and Antoni Slodkowski. It appeared on 8 February 2018. According to Al Jazeera's 2019 account, the two reporters found the grave and obtained pictures of the men before and after they were killed.

Wa Lone, then 31, and Kyaw Soe Oo, then 27, had been arrested on 12 December 2017 on the outskirts of Yangon. They were charged with possessing classified documents under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act, which carried up to 14 years in prison. Reuters said in its report that its investigation of Inn Din was what prompted the police to arrest them. The agency said they were innocent and had been arrested for doing their jobs. Judges denied them bail during the pre-trial hearings.

About a month after the arrests, the army issued what Al Jazeera called a rare statement admitting that security forces had taken part in extrajudicial killings of ten Rohingya "terrorists" in the village. NPR reporter Michael Sullivan said in December that the military acknowledged the grave because it knew the photographs were out there.

The reporters were later convicted. They were found guilty of breaching the Official Secrets Act and sentenced to seven years in prison under that law. During the trial, defence lawyers argued that the arrest and prosecution were meant to block their reporting. A police officer told the court that a senior officer had ordered the reporters to be set up and arrested. The two men spent more than 16 months behind bars before being released in an amnesty on 6 May 2019, according to Reuters as published by Al Jazeera.
content.h2: The army's trial of seven soldiers
content.p: In April 2018, after what it called an investigation, the army said that four officers and three other-ranking soldiers had been dismissed from service and given to 10 years with hard labour for "contributing and participating in murder". Neither their names nor their roles were disclosed. Radio Free Asia and Human Rights Watch later described the sentence as one of 10 years, and Radio Free Asia dated the court martial to March 2018. The reports do not agree on this point, so the date of the sentencing is uncertain.

Aung San Suu Kyi, the civilian leader, welcomed the convictions at the time, calling the sentencing Myanmar's "first step on the road of taking responsibility". The commander-in-chief, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, cited the case to visiting UN Security Council officials that April. "The latest crime we punished was a killing, and 10 years' imprisonment was given to seven perpetrators," he said, according to an account on his personal website. "We will not forgive anyone if they commit (a) crime."
One Buddhist villager was also jailed. Tun Aye, a school teacher, was, his lawyer Khin Win said, serving five years for murder in Buthidaung Prison when Reuters reported on the soldiers' release.

The seven soldiers did not serve the sentence. Reuters reported in May 2019, on the word of two prison officials, two former inmates and one of the soldiers, that they had been released in November 2018. A senior prison official in Naypyitaw said their punishment was "reduced by the military", but declined to give an exact date, and the release was never announced. Military spokesmen declined to comment.

Human Rights Watch said in 2020 that all seven had been pardoned by Min Aung Hlaing after serving just seven months. Radio Free Asia quoted a lawyer, Kyee Myint, as saying they spent nine months in prison, and Al Jazeera put it at less than one year. The sources differ on the length, so the time served cannot be stated precisely.

Former inmates described conditions that other prisoners lacked. Aung Than Wai, an activist who had been jailed in Sittwe under a privacy law, said the soldiers there were given beer and cigarettes. A second former inmate, who asked not to be named, said they were visited by army officials and that in November the seven were taken away in a military vehicle. A man named Zin Paing Soe confirmed to Reuters that he was one of the seven and was free. "We were told to shut up," he said. Reuters noted that a Facebook account he opened that month included a post about the end of a year he had mostly spent in jail.

Human Rights Watch accused the military in 2019 of a "massive cover-up of their crimes against humanity and genocide against the Rohingya". Its deputy South Asia director, Phil Robertson, said the early release showed that the commanders were never committed to seeing anyone held accountable.

The seven were the only security personnel the military had said it punished over the 2017 operation, according to Al Jazeera. Later, in November 2019, the army opened another court martial, over the killings of Rohingya near Gu Dar Pyin village. In June 2020 it announced three convictions without disclosing names, ranks or sentences. Human Rights Watch called that proceeding a sham and said the Inn Din convictions had been the only earlier ones for the 2017 abuses. Rights groups said that the military trials had delivered no justice for the Rohingya and were marred by procedural flaws and a lack of transparency, according to Radio Free Asia.

Myanmar's defenders of the process held a different view. At the International Court of Justice in December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi pointed to the Gu Dar Pyin court martial as evidence of the military's will to accountability, according to Human Rights Watch. Myanmar had also cited its military trials in testimony to the court, as evidence it could achieve accountability without outside interference, Radio Free Asia reported. For the families of the ten men from Inn Din, the case remained a story the army had acknowledged, then closed.
